data.text:
The US military's missiles, fighter jets, and submarines all depend on rare earth materials. China controls most of the global supply. The Pentagon just flew to Malaysia to fix that problem.

Lynas Rare Earths, an Australian company operating the world's largest rare earth processing plant outside China, has begun commercial production of heavy rare earth elements, specifically dysprosium, terbium, and samarium, at its facility in Kuantan, Malaysia. In March 2026, the US Department of Defense signed a $96 million, four-year supply agreement with Lynas to secure both light and heavy rare earth oxides for defense manufacturing.

Why does this matter? Dysprosium and terbium are essential components in the high-performance magnets inside F-35 fighter jets, Tomahawk missiles, Virginia-class submarines, and radar systems. Until Lynas began production in mid-2025, China had an effective monopoly over heavy rare earth processing globally.

The CCP demonstrated exactly how dangerous that monopoly is. In April 2025, China imposed export licensing requirements on seven heavy rare earth elements. Chinese magnet exports immediately fell by roughly three-quarters. European prices surged to six times Chinese domestic levels. Defense manufacturers scrambled. Automotive assembly lines slowed. China later suspended some restrictions as part of diplomatic negotiations, but the core licensing framework remains active and the suspension expires in November 2026.

This is not an accident or an overreaction. China controls around 70% of global rare earth production and over 90% of rare earth permanent magnet manufacturing. It has now proven, twice, that it is willing to weaponize that dominance when geopolitical pressure suits it.

Lynas in Malaysia is a genuine breakthrough. It is also still a small piece of what is needed. The US is years away from a fully independent domestic supply chain. The CCP knows the gap. The suspension of export controls is temporary. And the materials that go into the weapons defending Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines are still overwhelmingly processed in the country that considers all three of them problems to be solved.

LOOK: A thick layer of smog covers the capital as a prolonged fire at the Navotas sanitary landfill continues to affect air quality across Metro Manila.

Captured on April 27, the aerial view shows haze drifting over communities and major roads, reducing visibility and posing health risks. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources has ordered landfill operators to submit contingency plans for emergency response, nearly two weeks after the blaze began.

📷: Mark Balmores | MB

LOOK: Pedestrians wear face masks as they walk along Taft Avenue in Manila on Monday, April 27.

Air quality sensors across four monitored locations are recording “very unhealthy” levels, affecting much of the city and its nearby areas. Authorities attribute the deterioration in air quality to the ongoing fire at the Navotas sanitary landfill, with prevailing winds carrying smoke toward Manila and adjacent cities, raising health concerns among residents.

📷: Mark Balmores | MB
